library(readr)

tab_dir <- file.path("..", "results", "tables")

## 1. Aim, objectives and section map

The aim of this study is to comparatively evaluate the anti-trypanosomal
activity of methanolic extracts of the leaves, stem bark, roots and seeds of
*Azadirachta indica* and *Moringa oleifera* against *Trypanosoma congolense*
and *T. evansi* (thesis §1.8.1). Each specific objective (§1.8.2) is addressed
in a dedicated results section: extraction (i) in §5.1, phytochemical
characterisation (ii) in §5.2, the in-vitro motility assay (iii) in §5.3,
in-vivo infectivity monitoring (iv) in §5.4, and the comparative superiority
assessment (v) in §5.5. The analysis protocol, diagnostic checks and
limitations follow in §6–§7.

## 2. Data and experimental design

Source data are group means of n = 3 mice per group, parsed from Sheet 2 of
the study workbook into tidy CSVs (`analysis/data/`, builder
`analysis/R/01_build_datasets.R`). Within any plant × part × parasite block,
each of the 7 groups (five concentrations plus two controls) is therefore
n = 1 and supports description only. The analytical unit throughout is the
**block (N = 16; 8 per plant, 8 per parasite)**. Plant contrasts pair blocks
by part × parasite (8 pairs); parasite contrasts pair by plant × part
(8 pairs). Treatments appear as labelled in the source — Negative Control and
Positive Control, whose identities and doses are not stated in Sheet 2 — so
the Positive Control serves as an assay-validity reference only, not as a
non-inferiority comparator.

## 3. Endpoints

Parasitaemia is recorded on the ordinal LEV scale (0–5). Because day-40 LEV
proved degenerate (0 of 112 groups positive at day 40 — 68 zeros and 44
deaths — while positivity peaks near 30% around days 9–14), the primary
parasitaemia endpoint is the **AUC** (death-censored trapezoidal sum over
observed days, always reported alongside mortality), supported by peak LEV,
clearance day and day-40 status. Motility (+/−) is summarised per group as
time-to-immobilisation (TTI), proportion motile at t = 120 and mean proportion
motile; the source key defines only `+ Active motility` and `− No motility`
(`+-` is undefined and was set to NA, 2 cells). Body weight and PCV use
Δ = Post-Infection − Pre-Infection with literature-standard flags — anaemia at
Post PCV < 35% or ≥ 25% relative drop (severe: < 30% or ≥ 40%; Noyes et al.
2009; Naessens et al. 2005; Gitonga et al. 2017) and weight-toxicity signal at
≥ 10% loss (severe: ≥ 20%, the standard humane-endpoint range). Raw LEV
values above the 0–5 scale (42 cells: 41 decimals 5.01–5.3 plus one LEV = 6)
were capped to 5 with pre-cap values preserved (`lev_raw`) and flagged.
Missing in-vivo values are treated as animal death — an adopted convention,
since Sheet 2 never states it — and are never imputed.

## 4. Statistical methods

Descriptive analysis is primary: trajectory plots per block, endpoint tables,
and flag tabulations. Inference is entirely rank-based (LEV ordinal, N
small): Friedman tests blocked by block for ordered dose trends with pooled
Spearman ρ on log10(concentration) as the trend effect; paired Wilcoxon
signed-rank tests (exact where the data permit, otherwise the
continuity-corrected normal approximation — see §6) for dose-vs-control and
for plant/parasite contrasts, each with the matched-pairs rank-biserial
effect size (Cliff's delta family; |r| ≥ 0.11/0.28/0.43 small/medium/large
per Vargha & Delaney 2000) and the Hodges–Lehmann median difference with 95%
CI. The dose-vs-control Wilcoxons are the formal post-hoc family following
each omnibus trend test, Holm-adjusted per parasite; plant and parasite
contrasts address independent questions and are not corrected across
questions. Per-block trend tests at n = 1 have no power and pooled trend
tests would break independence, so only the blocked Friedman is reported as
inference. Significance is set at p < 0.05 with p-values supplementary to
effect sizes. All computation is in `analysis/R/02_analysis.R` (statistics
only, no machine learning).

## 5.1. Objective i — methanolic extraction

Objective i (extraction of leaves, stem bark, roots and seeds of both plants
under standard phytochemical protocols) is a laboratory procedure with no
statistical component: no yields or replicates are recorded in the available
data, so there is nothing to estimate or test. It is reported here only to
keep the objective map complete; efficacy inference begins with the
characterised extracts in §5.2–§5.5.

## 5.2. Objective ii — phytochemical contents

Screening detected all 12 assayed compound classes across the design, with
richness concentrated in leaves and seeds (@tbl-phyto). *M. oleifera*
leaves carry the broadest profile (9 of 12 classes present) while stem bark
in both plants is the sparsest fraction; no compound is unique to a single
plant part in a way that alone explains efficacy. Because only eight
plant × part combinations exist, these data support description only: the
presence matrix (@fig-phyto) is the result, and any compound–efficacy
association is an exploratory overlay tabulated without inference in
`phytochemical_efficacy_overlay.csv`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-phyto
#| tbl-cap: Phytochemical richness per plant and part (descriptive; screening data, no tests).
k("phytochemical_richness.csv")
```

![Phytochemical presence by plant and part](`r file.path(fig_dir, "phytochemical_heatmap.png")`){#fig-phyto}

## 5.3. Objective iii — in-vitro motility dose response

Motility collapses with both time and concentration in every block
(@fig-mot-traj): Negative Controls remain motile through 120 minutes while
100 mg/ml immobilises parasites within 15–30 minutes in most blocks, and the
recovered Positive Control rows show the expected rapid kill (+ at t = 0,
immobile thereafter). Group-level summaries (TTI, t120, mean proportion
motile; `endpoints_motility.csv`) confirm the pattern numerically — TTI is
derivable for 82 of 112 groups, the remainder being groups that never
immobilise (chiefly Negative Controls). The blocked dose–response test is
highly significant for both parasites (@tbl-mot-dose: *T. congolense*
Friedman Q = 27.75, p < 0.001, pooled ρ = −0.70; *T. evansi* Q = 30.32,
p < 0.001, ρ = −0.88), and mean AUC-equivalent motility falls monotonically
with log-concentration. Post-hoc dose-vs-control contrasts (@tbl-mot-posthoc)
show large, consistent effects at the top doses (rank-biserial −1; HL
reduction ≈ −0.83 for *congolense* 100 mg/ml and −0.89 for *evansi*
100 mg/ml) that sit just above the Holm-adjusted threshold (Holm 0.065 and
0.052) — strong but, at N = 8 blocks, formally inconclusive after
multiplicity control. Lower doses are indistinguishable from the control.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mot-dose
#| tbl-cap: Motility dose-response on mean proportion motile (Friedman blocked by block; Spearman on log10 dose).
k("dose_response_motility.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mot-posthoc
#| tbl-cap: Post-hoc motility contrasts, each dose vs Negative Control (paired Wilcoxon by block; Holm per parasite).
k("dose_vs_nc_motility.csv")
```

![Motility trajectories by block](`r file.path(fig_dir, "motility_trajectories_faceted.png")`){#fig-mot-traj}

## 5.4. Objective iv — in-vivo infectivity

### Parasitaemia

LEV trajectories rise from day 1, peak around days 9–14 and resolve toward
zero by day 40 in survivors (@fig-para-traj); mortality (44 of 112 groups
with at least one dead-animal day, first deaths days 9–37) accompanies the
decline, which is why AUC rather than day-40 LEV carries the inference.
Cumulative burden falls monotonically with concentration (@fig-auc),
significantly for *T. evansi* (@tbl-dose: Friedman Q = 14.51, p = 0.006,
pooled ρ = −0.51) and suggestively for *T. congolense* (Q = 8.52, p = 0.074,
ρ = −0.42). Post-hoc contrasts (@tbl-para-posthoc) confirm the gradient for
*T. evansi*: 100, 10 and 0.5 mg/ml each beat the Negative Control in all
eight blocks (W = 0, exact p = 0.008, Holm 0.039; HL ≈ −50/−50/−44 AUC-days),
while 0.01 and 0.005 mg/ml do not survive correction (Holm 0.078). For
*T. congolense* only 100 mg/ml is suggestive (p = 0.014, Holm 0.071) and no
dose is significant after correction. No parasite-level difference in AUC was
found (paired p = 0.46; @tbl-other).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dose
#| tbl-cap: Parasitaemia dose-response on AUC (Friedman blocked by block; Spearman on log10 dose).
k("dose_response.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-para-posthoc
#| tbl-cap: Post-hoc parasitaemia contrasts, each dose vs Negative Control on AUC (paired Wilcoxon by block; Holm per parasite).
k("dose_vs_nc_auc.csv")
```

![Mean AUC vs log10(concentration) by parasite](`r file.path(fig_dir, "auc_dose_response.png")`){#fig-auc}

![Parasitaemia trajectories by block](`r file.path(fig_dir, "parasitemia_trajectories_faceted.png")`){#fig-para-traj}

### Body weight and PCV

Weight and PCV deltas centre near zero with wide scatter (@fig-wt,
@fig-pcv); neither plant nor parasite contrasts approach significance
(@tbl-other: weight plant p = 0.31, parasite p = 0.15; PCV plant p = 0.74,
parasite p = 0.95). Toxicity and anaemia flags (`endpoints_weight.csv`,
`endpoints_pcv.csv`) are therefore the substantive read-out: they identify
the groups paying a physiological price for infection regardless of
treatment, consistent with efficacy that is parasitological rather than
confounded by differential toxicity.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-other
#| tbl-cap: Parasite, weight and PCV contrasts (paired Wilcoxon; 8 pairs each).
k("parasite_comparison.csv")
k("weight_tests.csv")
k("pcv_tests.csv")
```

![Body-weight change Post−Pre (g)](`r file.path(fig_dir, "weight_delta_boxplot.png")`){#fig-wt}

![PCV change Post−Pre (pp)](`r file.path(fig_dir, "pcv_delta_boxplot.png")`){#fig-pcv}

## 5.5. Objective v — comparative superiority

There is no evidence that either plant is superior. Block-mean AUC pairs
scatter on both sides of identity (@fig-paired): paired W = 14, exact
p = 1.0, HL ≈ 0.3 AUC-days with 95% CI (−14.7, +20.5), rank-biserial −0.14
(@tbl-sup). The motility cross-check agrees (paired p = 0.15, HL 0.11).
With only eight pairs the interval spans effects in both directions, so the
data cannot support a superiority claim for either agent; the correct
conclusion is the null, stated with its confidence interval rather than as a
bare p-value.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sup
#| tbl-cap: Plant superiority contrasts (paired Wilcoxon; 8 pairs each).
k("plant_superiority.csv")
k("plant_superiority_motility.csv")
```

![Paired block-mean AUC: A. indica vs M. oleifera](`r file.path(fig_dir, "plant_paired_auc.png")`){#fig-paired}

## 6. Diagnostics, sensitivity and refits

Three diagnostics were run and each changed or confirmed the analysis.
First, rank-test validity: several contrasts contain tied absolute
differences (all five *T. congolense* dose contrasts; most motility
contrasts, whose endpoint averages nine binary points) or dropped zero
differences (plant superiority: one of eight pairs). Because R's exact
Wilcoxon distribution is invalid with tied ranks, every contrast now records
`n_nonzero`, `n_ties` and `p_method`, using the exact p-value only when
neither occurs and the continuity-corrected normal approximation otherwise —
this refit left all conclusions unchanged (e.g. *congolense* 100 mg/ml:
asymptotic p = 0.014, Holm 0.071). Second, paired-difference symmetry, the
remaining signed-rank assumption, was inspected visually (@fig-sym): the
*evansi* differences sit entirely below zero (a location shift, unproblematic
for the test), while the superiority differences spread symmetrically around
zero, matching its null result. Third, leave-one-block-out sensitivity
(@tbl-loo) shows every headline claim is stable — no single block flips any
conclusion (evansi top doses: LOO p = 0.016 throughout; superiority null:
LOO p 0.53–1.0). Completeness was verified structurally (4480/336/336/1008/96
rows with 4 part levels enforced at build).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-loo
#| tbl-cap: Leave-one-block-out sensitivity of headline claims (stable = no single block flips the conclusion).
k("sensitivity_loo.csv")
```

![Paired differences: symmetry check (red = median)](`r file.path(fig_dir, "diagnostic_paired_diffs.png")`){#fig-sym}

## 7. Limitations

Each CSV row is a mean of n = 3 mice, so no within-group variance survives
and all inference rests on N = 16 blocks (8 per contrast) — power is low,
intervals are wide, and descriptive patterns carry the weight. Control
identities and doses are unknown in the source, so the Positive Control is a
validity reference, not a comparator. Death-censored AUC favours early-death
groups numerically, hence every AUC is read alongside mortality. NA = death
is an adopted convention worth confirming against the animal records. All
results are exploratory, not confirmatory.
